name: Aaron Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a certified translator, Polish into English, so most of my work is official papers: birth certificates, marriage certificates, school diplomas, driving licences. Each one gets my stamp and signature, which the courts and the passport office accept. I work from a desk in my parents' back room, because I'm saving for my wedding to Kasia next summer. On Sundays after Mass I often help Polish families at the parish fill in council forms, for free.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work with a stamp on it; if I get it wrong, my name is on it. What's hard is the money. People bring in one birth certificate at a time and pay thirty-five each, and there are only so many Polish families in a town this size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that people got carried away. Folk at the parish would nod and say they never trusted computers anyway. I wouldn't post about it; I'm not really online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but my problems are the same as now. Thirty-five a certificate, a wedding to pay for and maybe two weeks' money in the bank. The stamp protects me, but it doesn't make me rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the certificates and ask the solicitors on Market Street if they'd send me their Polish clients. I'd cut back on going out until the wedding's paid. I wouldn't touch the AI tools; I don't need them for a birth certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's a bit of a knot about the wedding bills, but that's ordinary life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked the solicitors before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, partly. My dad always said good work finds its own customers. But my fiancée Kasia says that's how you stay poor, and she's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's paying for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly us, with help from both families. Kasia's dad offered to pay for the hall, which is a big help. I'd like to pay for the rest myself, as a matter of pride.

say: People got **carried away** with the hype about AI.
Folk at the parish **never trusted** computers anyway, and they'd say so.
think: The **stamp** protects me, but it doesn't make me rich.
My worries are **thirty-five a certificate** and the wedding.
do: Ask the **Market Street solicitors** for their Polish clients.
Cut back on **going out** until the wedding's paid.
feel: **Mostly settled**, with a knot about wedding bills.
S0.quote: My dad always said good work finds its own customers. But my fiancée Kasia says that's how you stay poor, and she's probably right.
fieldNote: His certified **stamp** gives him more legal protection than most translators.
Money stress is about the **wedding** and low per-document pay.
Proud and **self-reliant**; he wants to pay his own way.

steps.text: Ask the Market Street solicitors to send him their Polish clients
Stop going out until the wedding is paid for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and you can't stop the market. But I'd also say that a certificate for a court needs a person who signs and takes the blame. That's not something you hand to a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the stamp keeps me going for a few years, but the official bodies might start accepting AI translations with a quick check. Then I'm thirty-five down a certificate with nothing to replace it. That would worry me a lot with the wedding coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the certified work while the rules protect it. I'd talk to my uncle Tomasz about his roofing firm, in case I needed a fallback. And I'd keep the wedding small, maybe fifty guests instead of a hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. I picked a job with a stamp because I thought that made it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a roofing job mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's honest work, like mine, just colder. My uncle Tomasz has said for years there's a place for me. I'd hate the heights, but I'd do it if it kept us going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not putting my name on something a computer wrote. If I sign a certificate, I want to know every word came from me.

A court certificate needs a person who **signs** and takes the **blame**.
think: The **stamp** keeps me going a few years, then maybe not.

Talk to his uncle about **roofing** as a fallback.
Keep the wedding small, **fifty guests** instead of a hundred.
feel: **Uncomfortable**: he chose a job with a stamp to be safe.
S1.quote: I'm not putting my name on something a computer wrote. If I sign a certificate, I want to know every word came from me.
fieldNote: Free-market in principle, but relies on **legal protection** for his stamp.
Turns to **family**, not the state, for a fallback.
Refuses AI on **personal integrity** grounds, not fear.

steps.text: Keep the certified certificate work while the rules require a stamp
Ask uncle Tomasz about a place at his roofing firm
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to fifty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after their own and each other. I don't want the government running everyone's lives, but this is too fast for anyone. I'd say it at church and to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if AI can do all thinking work by 2028, the stamp won't last. Some minister will change the rules to save money. My job's all thinking, so I'd be out quickly; roofing would give me about three years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle Tomasz straight away and start as a labourer, learning the trade. I'd keep doing certificates in the evenings while they still need a stamp. Kasia and I would push the wedding back a year so we're not borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'd pray about it, honestly. It's the kind of thing you can't fix on your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would pushing back the wedding mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt. My fiancée Kasia's grandmother is 88 and wants to see our wedding. But I'm not starting married life in debt. That's how my parents raised me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said roofing gives you three years. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe by then there's something else. I'm not going to pretend I have it figured out, I'd just do the next right thing.

say: People need to **look after their own** and each other.
I don't want **government running lives**, but this is too fast.
think: Some minister will change the rules and the **stamp won't last**.
**Roofing** gives me about three years longer.
do: Start as a **labourer** at uncle Tomasz's roofing firm.
Do **certificates** in the evenings while stamps are needed.
Push the **wedding** back a year to avoid borrowing.
S2.quote: My fiancée Kasia's grandmother is 88 and wants to see our wedding. But I'm not starting married life in debt.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose translation** fast and switch to hands-on work.
**Family and faith** carry the plan, not public support.
Postponing the wedding shows the **real cost** at his life stage.

steps.text: Start labouring at uncle Tomasz's roofing firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families and communities to get ready. I'd tell the young lads at church to learn a trade. I'd not say much beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get three or four years of certificates before the rules change. That's long enough to get married and maybe learn roofing properly. I'd still be losing the job I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on certificates for now and do the wedding as planned, small. In year two I'd start a roofing apprenticeship with my uncle, weekends first. I'd put every spare bit aside after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see how it goes. That's better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tell the young lads to learn a trade, rather than yourself now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I suppose I'm hoping the stamp lasts. But you're right, I should listen to my own advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad is a plumber and thinks translating is sitting down for a living. He'd say a man should be able to fix a roof anyway.

I'd tell the young lads at church to **learn a trade**.
think: I'd get **three or four years** of certificates before rules change.
I'd still be **losing the job** I trained for.
do: Keep the **wedding** as planned, but small.
Start a weekend **roofing apprenticeship** in year two.
**Save** every spare bit after the wedding.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to see how it goes.
S3.quote: My dad is a plumber and thinks translating is sitting down for a living. He'd say a man should be able to fix a roof anyway.
fieldNote: He gives others advice he's **slow to take** himself, and admits it.
Five years lets him **marry first**, then switch.
His father's **trade pride** shapes how he sees the switch.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. That sounds hard, but I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have most of the decade on certificates if the rules hold. I'd be married, maybe with a child. That's exactly when losing an income would hurt most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with certificates and wait a few years to see how the rules go. I'd start saving properly after the wedding. If the passport office ever starts accepting AI, I'd go to my uncle the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though I know I'm leaning on the stamp. And robots for roofs come by 2039 anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who don't prepare have themselves to blame. Are you preparing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. I'm waiting. I'd say I'm preparing to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do children fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want two children, God willing. I'd want our children to have a dad with a steady wage. That's what this is really about for me.

say: **Ten years** is plenty of time for anyone to prepare.
Anyone who doesn't prepare has **only themselves** to blame, hard as that sounds.
think: I'd have most of the decade on **certificates** if rules hold.
I'd be married, maybe with a **child**, when the income goes.
do: Carry on with **certificates** and watch the rules.
Go to his uncle the week **AI is accepted**.
feel: **Calmer**, while knowing he's leaning on the stamp.
S4.quote: We want two children, God willing. I'd want our children to have a dad with a steady wage.
fieldNote: He judges others harshly but admits he's **preparing to prepare**.
Future **children** are what's really at stake for him.
Notes that **robots for roofs** cut his fallback short too.

steps.text: Keep doing certificates while official bodies require a stamp
Save properly once the wedding is paid off
Join uncle Tomasz's roofing firm if AI translations are accepted

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The wedding, no money, and my trade gone in two years. What would help is clear rules that keep a signed human translation for official papers, and apprenticeships that take people my age, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the Polish families at church. The Polish families at church trust me because I'm one of them. A machine doesn't come to Mass.

headlineQuote: The Polish families at church trust me because I'm one of them. A machine doesn't come to Mass.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** certified Polish–English translator saving for his wedding to Kasia.
He works from his **parents' back room** and earns about thirty-five a certificate.
He never uses AI and **won't sign** anything a computer wrote.
Traditional and self-reliant, he turns to **family and faith**, especially uncle Tomasz's roofing firm.
He admits he'd **wait too long** when given ten years, but moves fast if given two.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his trade would go just as his marriage starts.
whatWouldHelp: Rules keeping **signed human translations** for official papers.
**Apprenticeships** that take people his age, not handouts.
